question: The base-ten representation for \(19!\) is \(121,\) \(6T5,\) \(100,\) \(40M,\) \(832,\) \(H00,\) where \(T,\) \(M,\) and \(H\) denote digits that are not given. What is \(T+M+H?\)
solution:
The divisibility properties of \(19!\) determine the missing digits without computing the entire factorial.

Among \(1,2,\ldots,19\), only \(5,10,15\) contribute factors of \(5\), one each. There are more than three factors of \(2\), so \(19!\) ends in exactly three zeros. Hence \(H=0\).

Because \(19!\) is divisible by \(9\), its digit sum
\[
T+M+33
\]
is a multiple of \(9\). Since \(0\le T+M\le18\), this sum lies between \(33\) and \(51\). The possible multiples are \(36\) and \(45\), so
\[
T+M=3\quad\text{or}\quad T+M=12.
\]
Also, \(19!\) is divisible by \(11\). The divisibility test for \(11\) says that the difference between the sums of alternating digits is a multiple of \(11\). Here that difference is
\[
(T+13)-(M+20)=T-M-7.
\]
It lies between \(-16\) and \(2\), so it must be \(-11\) or \(0\). Therefore
\[
T-M=-4\quad\text{or}\quad T-M=7.
\]
If \(T+M=3\), both digits are at most \(3\), making either possible difference impossible. Thus \(T+M=12\). The difference \(T-M=7\) would then give \(2T=19\), impossible for an integer digit. Consequently,
\[
T+M=12,\qquad T-M=-4,
\]
which gives \(T=4\) and \(M=8\). Hence
\[
\boxed{T+M+H=4+8+0=12},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
